p.src: This lyric, sung to the tune “Immortal by the River,” tells only how Tang Sanzang and his three disciples brought water and fire into harmony and restored their true nature to cool serenity. They had borrowed the precious fan of pure yin, fanned out the scorching flames, and crossed the mountain. Before many days had passed, they had covered the full eight hundred li; master and disciples journeyed carefree and at ease, continuing westward. p.src: After the four travelers had journeyed for a long while, they again drew near a walled city. Tang Sanzang reined in his horse and called to his disciple, “Wukong, look at those imposing towers and pavilions. What place might that be?” The Pilgrim raised his head and looked; it was indeed a walled city. Truly it was a sight such as this:

p.src: The Pilgrim said, “Master, that city is the seat of an emperor.” Bajie laughed and said, “Every prefecture under Heaven has its prefectural city, and every county its county town. How can you tell at a glance that this is an emperor’s seat?” The Pilgrim said, “You do not understand. An emperor’s residence is naturally different from a prefecture or county. Look: on its four sides are more than ten gates, its circuit extends over a hundred li, its towers and terraces soar aloft, and many-colored clouds and mists gather about them. If this were not an imperial capital, how could it possess such splendor?” Friar Sand said, “Elder Brother, keen-eyed as you are, you may recognize it as an emperor’s seat, but what is the place called?” The Pilgrim said, “There is neither signboard nor banner here. How could I know? We must enter the city and ask before we can find out.”

p.src: The elder urged his horse onward and soon reached the gate. He dismounted, crossed the bridge, and entered the gate to look about. They saw the busy streets and markets, where goods circulated and wealth changed hands; they also saw splendidly dressed citizens and people of prosperous bearing. As they went on, they suddenly saw more than ten monks, each wearing a cangue and chains, begging from door to door, their clothes truly ragged beyond description. Sanzang sighed, “When the rabbit dies, the fox grieves; creatures mourn the suffering of their own kind.” Then he called, “Wukong, go forward and ask them why they are suffering so.” Obeying him, the Pilgrim called out at once, “You monks there, from which monastery do you come? For what offense are you wearing cangues and chains?” The monks fell to their knees and said, “Good sir, we are monks of Golden Light Monastery who have been falsely accused.” The Pilgrim asked, “Where is Golden Light Monastery?” The monks replied, “It is just around the corner.” The Pilgrim led them before Tang Sanzang and asked, “How were you wronged? Tell me your story.” The monks said, “Good sirs, we do not know where you have come from, but your faces seem somehow familiar to us. We dare not explain it here. Please come to our humble monastery, and there we shall tell you all our suffering.” The elder said, “Quite so. Let us go to their monastery and inquire closely into the cause.”

p.src: Sanzang’s heart ached, and he could not keep the tears from his eyes. Still bearing their cangues and chains, the monks pushed open the main hall and invited the elder to enter and worship the Buddha. The elder entered the hall, offered the incense of his heart, and clicked his teeth three times. Then he went around to the rear and saw another six or seven young monks chained to the pillars beneath the abbot’s eaves. Sanzang could scarcely bear the sight.

p.src: When they reached the abbot’s quarters, all the monks came and kowtowed, asking, “Good sirs, each of you has an uncommon appearance. Can it be that you have come from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land?” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “What art of foreknowledge do you monks possess? That is exactly where we are from. How did you recognize us?” The monks replied, “Good sir, what art of foreknowledge could we possibly possess? It is only that we suffer bitter injustice and have nowhere to clear our names, so day after day we cry out to Heaven and Earth. Perhaps we moved the heavenly gods, for last night each of us had a dream saying that a holy monk from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land would save our lives and enable this bitter injustice to be redressed. Today, seeing your extraordinary appearances just as foretold, we recognized you.”

p.src: Sanzang was delighted to hear this and said, “What place is this? And what injustice have you suffered?” The monks knelt and reported, “Good sir, this city is called the Kingdom of Jisai, a great realm of the Western Regions. In former years, four foreign lands sent tribute: to the south, the Kingdom of Yuetuo; to the north, the Kingdom of Gaochang; to the east, the Kingdom of Western Liang; and to the west, the Kingdom of Benbo. Every year they offered fine jade, lustrous pearls, beautiful consorts, and noble steeds as tribute. Without our raising arms or marching out to punish them, they naturally revered us as the sovereign realm.” Sanzang said, “Since they revered your land as their sovereign realm, I suppose your king was virtuous and his civil and military officials were worthy men.” The monks said, “Good sir, neither the civil officials nor the military ones are worthy, and the sovereign is no virtuous ruler. From ancient times the precious pagoda of our Golden Light Monastery was wreathed in auspicious clouds and crowned with rising blessed vapors: by night it emitted a rosy radiance that people ten thousand li away had seen; by day it sent forth multicolored vapors, which all four kingdoms gazed upon alike. Thus they regarded this as a heavenly seat and divine capital, and the four foreign lands came to pay tribute. But three years ago, on the first day of the seventh month, at midnight, a rain of blood fell. At daybreak, every household was afraid and every family was plunged into sorrow. All the ministers and nobles memorialized the king, not knowing what offense had drawn Heaven’s rebuke. Taoist priests were invited to perform rites, and Buddhist monks to recite scriptures, in answer to Heaven and thanksgiving to Earth. But who could have known that the golden pagoda in our monastery had been defiled? For the past two years, the foreign kingdoms have ceased to bring tribute. Our king wished to launch a punitive expedition, but his ministers remonstrated that the monks of our monastery had stolen the treasure from the pagoda, and that this was why the auspicious clouds and blessed vapors had vanished and the foreign kingdoms no longer attended court. The benighted ruler made no further inquiry into the truth. Those corrupt officials seized our community of monks and subjected us to every kind of torture and endless interrogation. At the time there were three generations of monks here. The first two could not endure the torture and died; now they have arrested our generation as well, charged us with the crime, and put us in cangues and chains. With you above us as our witness, good sir, how could we ever violate our consciences by stealing the treasure from the pagoda? We beg you, good sirs, to take pity on us. As things gather by kind and creatures flock with their own, please exercise your great mercy and compassion, display your vast spiritual powers, and save our lives.”

p.src: Hearing this, Sanzang nodded and sighed, “This affair is obscure and difficult to fathom. On the one hand, the court has governed badly; on the other, calamity has befallen you. Since Heaven sent down a rain of blood that defiled the precious pagoda, why did you not memorialize the sovereign at the time? Why let matters come to such suffering?” The monks said, “Good sir, we are mere mortals. How could we know Heaven’s will? Even our predecessors could not discern the truth, so what could we have done?” Sanzang asked, “Wukong, what time is it now?” The Pilgrim replied, “It is about the hour of the monkey.” Sanzang said, “I wish to appear before the sovereign and have our travel rescript exchanged, but until the affair of these monks is clarified, I shall find it difficult to make a report to him. When I left Chang’an, I made a vow at Famen Monastery: on my journey to the Western Heaven, whenever I met a shrine I would burn incense, whenever I encountered a monastery I would worship the Buddha, and whenever I saw a pagoda I would sweep it. Today I have arrived here and found monks suffering injustice because of a precious pagoda. Find me a new broom. After I have bathed, I shall go up and sweep the pagoda, examine how it came to be defiled and why it no longer shines, and seek out the truth. Only then can I properly report the matter to the sovereign and deliver these monks from their suffering.”

p.src: When the monks in cangues and chains heard this, they hurried to the kitchen, fetched a kitchen knife, and handed it to Eight Rules, saying, “Grandfather, use this knife to break the iron locks binding the young monks to the pillars. Release them so they may prepare a vegetarian meal and fragrant bathwater, and attend upon the reverend masters while they dine and bathe. Meanwhile, we shall go into the streets and beg for some new brooms with which the reverend masters may sweep the pagoda.” Eight Rules laughed. “What is so difficult about opening locks? There is no need for knife or axe. Ask that hairy-faced master of mine—he is an old hand at opening locks.” Pilgrim duly stepped forward, worked a lock-opening spell, and swept his hand across them; all the locks fell away at once. The young monks all ran to the kitchen, scrubbed the pots and stoves clean, and prepared tea and food. By the time Tripitaka and his disciples had finished their vegetarian meal, dusk was gradually falling. Presently the monks in cangues and chains returned carrying two brooms, much to Tripitaka’s delight.

p.src: When Tripitaka had finished bathing, he put on a narrow-sleeved short robe, fastened a ringed sash around his waist, changed into a pair of soft official shoes, and took a new broom in his hand. He said to the monks, “You may all retire for the night. I am going to sweep the pagoda.” Pilgrim said, “The pagoda has been defiled by a rain of blood, and moreover it has stood dark for a long time, so I fear that evil things may have bred within it. Besides, the night is still and the wind is cold, and you have no companion. I fear some mishap if you go alone. How would it be if old Monkey went up with you?” “Excellent, excellent,” said Tripitaka. Each carrying a broom, the two first went into the great hall, lit the glazed lamp, burned incense, and bowed before the Buddha, praying, “Your disciple Chen Xuanzang, commissioned by the Great Tang of the Eastern Land to journey to Vulture Peak and seek scriptures from our Buddha the Tathagata, has now reached the Golden Ray Monastery in the Kingdom of Jisai. Here the monks have told me that the precious pagoda was defiled and that the king, suspecting them of stealing its treasure, condemned them unjustly, leaving high and low alike unable to clear their names. Your disciple will sweep the pagoda with all sincerity. I pray that our Buddha, in his divine power, will swiftly reveal the cause of its defilement and not allow innocent mortals to suffer injustice.” When the prayer was over, he and Pilgrim opened the pagoda door and began sweeping upward from the lowest storey. And this pagoda was truly a sight to behold:

p.src: The Tang Monk swept one storey and then climbed to the next. In this fashion they had swept as far as the seventh storey when it was already the second watch. The elder gradually grew weary, and Pilgrim said, “If you are tired, sit down for a while and let old Monkey finish the sweeping for you.” “How many storeys does this pagoda have?” asked Tripitaka. “Surely no fewer than thirteen,” Pilgrim replied. Burdened by fatigue, the elder said, “We must sweep it all clean if I am to fulfill my vow.” After sweeping three more storeys, his back ached and his legs were sore. He sank down on the tenth storey and said, “Wukong, sweep the remaining three storeys clean for me.” Pilgrim roused his spirits, climbed to the eleventh storey, and in a moment had gone on to the twelfth. As he was sweeping, he suddenly heard voices on the top of the pagoda. “Strange!” said Pilgrim. “How strange! It is nearly the third watch—how can anyone be talking up there at this hour? It must surely be some evil creature. I shall go and see.”

p.src: Good Monkey King! Quietly tucking the broom under his arm, he hitched up his robe, slipped out through the front opening, and stepped onto a cloud to take a look. There in the center of the thirteenth storey sat two fiends. Before them were a plate of food, a bowl, and a wine pot, and they were playing drinking games as they drank. Pilgrim worked his magic, cast aside the broom, drew out his gold-banded staff, barred the pagoda door, and shouted, “So, monsters! You are the ones who stole the treasure from the pagoda!” The two monsters panicked, leapt to their feet, and hurled pot and bowl about wildly. Pilgrim held them back with his iron staff laid crosswise and said, “If I beat you to death, there will be no one left to confess.” He merely pressed the staff toward them. The monsters were pinned against the wall and could not struggle free in the least. They could only cry, “Spare our lives! Spare our lives! It had nothing to do with us. The one who stole the treasure is elsewhere!” Pilgrim used a grappling spell, seized one in each hand, and carried them straight down to the tenth storey, announcing, “Master, I have caught the thieves who stole the treasure.” Tripitaka had been dozing. Hearing this suddenly, he was both startled and delighted. “Where did you catch them?” he asked. Pilgrim hauled the monsters before him and forced them to their knees. “They were drinking and playing finger-guessing games on top of the pagoda. Old Monkey heard the commotion, sprang onto a cloud, leapt to the summit, and barred their way. I did not use any force, for I feared that one blow would kill them and leave no one to confess. That is why I captured them gently. Master, question them and take their testimony. Find out what sort of fiends they are, where they come from, and where the stolen treasure is hidden.”

p.src: The monsters trembled all over, crying for mercy, and then made a full confession. “We two were sent to patrol the pagoda by the All-Saints Dragon King of Emerald Wave Pool at Tumbledown Rock Mountain. He is called Benbo’erba, and I am called Babo’erben. He is a catfish fiend, and I am a snakehead spirit. Our old All-Saints Dragon had a daughter named the All-Saints Princess. The princess has the beauty of flowers and the moon and is more than twice as gifted as ordinary women. She took a consort called the Nine-Headed Prince Consort, whose magic powers are immense. The year before last, he came here with the Dragon King, displayed his mighty magic, brought down a shower of blood that defiled the precious pagoda, and stole the Buddha’s relic treasure from within it. The princess also went up to the Great Cinnabar Heaven, to the front of the Hall of Miraculous Mist, and stole the Queen Mother’s nine-leaf divine fungus. It is nurtured beneath the pool, filling the place with golden light and rosy radiance so that it shines by day and night. Recently we heard that a Sun Wukong was journeying west to fetch the scriptures. They say his magic powers are great and that all along the road he makes a special business of finding fault with others. So of late we have often been sent here to patrol and spy. If Sun Wukong should arrive, they want to be ready for him.” Hearing this, Pilgrim gave a cold chuckle. “Those vile beasts are utterly outrageous! No wonder they invited the Bull Demon King to a banquet there the other day. So they have been consorting with that band of wicked demons and devoting themselves to evil deeds.”

Recently we heard that a Sun Wukong was journeying west to fetch the scriptures. They say his magic powers are great and that all along the road he makes a special business of finding fault with others. So of late we have often been sent here to patrol and spy. If Sun Wukong should arrive, they want to be ready for him.”

Hearing this, Pilgrim gave a cold chuckle. “Those vile beasts are utterly outrageous! No wonder they invited the Bull Demon King to a banquet there the other day. So they have been consorting with that band of wicked demons and devoting themselves to evil deeds.”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, Eight Rules appeared with two or three young monks, carrying two lanterns up from below the pagoda. “Master,” he said, “you have finished sweeping the pagoda, yet instead of going to sleep, what are you discussing up here?” Pilgrim said, “Brother, you have come at just the right time. It was the old All-Saints Dragon who stole the treasure from the pagoda. Now he had sent these two little fiends to patrol the pagoda and spy out news of our arrival, but I caught them just now.” “What are their names?” asked Eight Rules. “What kind of fiends are they?” Pilgrim replied, “They have just made their confession. One is called Benbo’erba, and the other Babo’erben. One is a catfish fiend, and the other a snakehead spirit.” Eight Rules drew his rake and made to strike them. “Since they are fiends and we have their confession, what are we waiting for? Why not beat them to death?” “You do not understand,” said Pilgrim. “Keep them alive for now, so they can testify before the emperor. They can also serve as guides to help us find the thieves and recover the treasure.” Good idiot! He actually lowered his rake, and each of the two brothers seized one monster and dragged it down the pagoda. The monsters kept crying, “Spare our lives!” Eight Rules said, “We need your catfish and snakehead flesh to make some fresh soup for those monks who have suffered unjustly.”

p.src: Two or three young monks joyfully took up lanterns and led the elder down from the pagoda. One ran ahead to tell the other monks, “All is well! All is well! We shall see the light of day again—the fiends who stole the treasure have already been caught and brought here by our saviors.” Pilgrim ordered, “Bring iron chains, pierce their shoulder blades, and shackle them here. You are to guard them while we go to sleep. We shall deal with them tomorrow.” The monks kept close watch and let Tripitaka and his disciples retire for the night.

p.src: Before they knew it, dawn had broken. The elder said, “Wukong and I shall go to court and have our travel document certified.” The elder put on his brocade cassock and Vairocana cap, composed himself with due dignity, and strode forward. Pilgrim tightened his tigerskin kilt, straightened his cotton robe, took the travel document, and went with him. Eight Rules asked, “Why aren’t you taking those two demon thieves along?” Pilgrim replied, “Once we have reported the matter, an imperial warrant will naturally be issued for men to fetch them.” They then proceeded to the palace gate. There was no end to the splendor of vermilion birds and yellow dragons, the serene celestial court and crimson palace towers. Arriving at the Donghua Gate, Tripitaka bowed to the gate commissioner and said, “May I trouble Your Excellency to report that this humble monk was sent from the Great Tang in the eastern land to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. I wish to have audience with the king and obtain certification of my travel document.” The chamberlain duly announced them, going before the steps to report, “Outside are two monks of strange appearance and dress. They say they were sent by the Tang court in the eastern land of Southern Jambudvipa to worship the Buddha and seek scriptures in the West, and that they wish to pay court to Your Majesty and have their travel document certified.”

p.src: On hearing this, the king issued an order for them to be admitted. The elder immediately led Pilgrim into court. At the sight of Pilgrim, every civil and military official was terrified. Some called him a monkey monk, while others called him a monk with the beak of the Thunder Duke. All shuddered and dared not look at him for long. Before the steps, the elder performed the ceremonial motions, hailed the sovereign, and bowed. The Great Sage merely clasped his hands and stood at an angle to one side, openly refusing to move. The elder memorialized, “Your Majesty’s monk-subject was sent by the Great Tang in the eastern land of Southern Jambudvipa to worship the Buddha at the Great Thunderclap Monastery in India of the West and obtain the true scriptures. As our road passes through your honored realm, we dared not proceed without leave. We carry a travel document and beg that it be checked and certified before we continue.” The king was delighted to hear this and ordered that the holy monk from the Tang be summoned onto the Golden Throne Hall, where an embroidered stool was set for him to sit upon. The elder went into the hall alone, first presented the travel document with both hands, and then, after thanking the king for his grace, ventured to sit.

p.src: The king read through the travel document and said with pleasure, “When your Tang emperor fell ill, he was able to choose an eminent monk who, undaunted by the great distance, would worship the Buddha and fetch scriptures; but the monks here in my realm devote themselves solely to thievery, bringing ruin to the country and their sovereign.” Hearing this, Tripitaka joined his palms and asked, “How have they brought ruin to the country and its sovereign?” The king replied, “My realm is a foremost nation of the Western Regions, and peoples from all four borders once regularly brought tribute. This was because within the kingdom stood the Golden Ray Monastery, containing a precious golden pagoda from whose summit radiance soared to the sky. Recently, thieving monks of that very monastery secretly stole the treasure within. For three years the radiance has been gone, and for those same three years the foreign lands have ceased to pay court. This fills me with grief and hatred.” Tripitaka joined his palms and said with a smile, “Your Majesty, ‘An error of a hair’s breadth may lead one a thousand miles astray.’ When this humble monk reached your celestial capital last night, the moment I entered the city gate I saw more than ten monks wearing cangues and fetters. When I asked their crime, they said they were the innocent sufferers from the Golden Ray Monastery. I therefore went to the monastery and investigated carefully; the matter had nothing at all to do with its monks. This humble monk swept the pagoda after nightfall and has already captured the demon thieves who stole the treasure.” The king cried with delight, “Where are the demon thieves?” Tripitaka replied, “They are now chained up by my young disciple in the Golden Ray Monastery.”

p.src: The king hastily issued a golden warrant: “Let the Embroidered Uniform Guard hurry to the Golden Ray Monastery, fetch the demon thieves, and bring them here for my personal interrogation.” Tripitaka memorialized again, “Your Majesty, though you have the Embroidered Uniform Guard, my young disciple must go with them.” The king asked, “Where is your worthy disciple?” Pointing with his hand, Tripitaka said, “He is the one standing beside the jade steps.” When the king saw him, he exclaimed in astonishment, “The holy monk has so noble a bearing—why does your worthy disciple look like that?” Hearing this, the Great Sage Sun shouted sternly, “Your Majesty, ‘A man cannot be judged by his looks, nor the sea measured with a bushel.’ If you care only for handsome looks, how could the demon thieves ever be caught?” At these words the king’s astonishment turned to delight, and he said, “The holy monk speaks truly. We do not choose men here by appearance; what matters above all is that the thieves be captured and the treasure recovered and restored to the pagoda.” He further ordered the master of the imperial equipage to prepare a carriage and canopy, and told the Embroidered Uniform Guard to attend the holy monk well as they went to fetch the demon thieves. The officer at once prepared a great sedan chair and a yellow parasol. The Embroidered Uniform Guard mustered its guardsmen, seated Pilgrim in the chair borne by eight men, cleared the road with four mighty shouts, and proceeded straight to the Golden Ray Monastery. This stirred the entire city, and there was not a single place where people did not flock to see the holy monk and the demon thieves.

p.src: When Eight Rules and Sha Monk heard the cries clearing the road, they assumed the king had sent officials and hurried out to receive them, only to discover Pilgrim seated in the sedan chair. The idiot laughed to his face and said, “Brother, you have regained your proper station!” Pilgrim got out of the chair, took Eight Rules by the arm, and asked, “How have I regained my proper station?” Eight Rules replied, “You have a yellow parasol over you and ride in a chair borne by eight men—is that not precisely the dignity due a Monkey King? That is why I said you had regained your proper station.” Pilgrim said, “Enough of your jokes.” He then unchained the two monsters to escort them before the king. Sha Monk said, “Brother, let your little brother share in the honor too.” Pilgrim replied, “You stay here and guard the luggage and horses.” The monks in cangues and fetters said, “You gentlemen should all go and receive the emperor’s favor. Let us remain here and keep watch.” Pilgrim said, “In that case, wait until I have reported your situation to the king; then I shall return and release you.” Eight Rules seized one demon thief and Sha Monk the other. The Great Sage Sun resumed his seat in the sedan chair, the procession formed up, and the two monsters were escorted to the royal court.

p.src: Presently, they reached the white jade steps and reported to the king, “The demon thieves have been brought here.” The king descended from his dragon throne and, together with the Tang Monk and all his civil and military officials, looked them over. One monster had bulging gills, black scales, a pointed snout, and sharp teeth; the other had slick skin, a great belly, a huge mouth, and long whiskers. Though they had feet and could walk, they had evidently assumed human form. The king asked, “What region are you thieving monsters from, and what place spawned you fiends? For how many years have you plagued my realm, and in what year did you steal my treasure? How many villains are there in your band, and what are all their names? Confess every detail truthfully.” The two monsters knelt before the throne, their necks streaming with blood, yet they seemed insensible to pain. They confessed, “Three years ago, on the first day of the seventh month, a Dragon King of All Saints led many of his kin to settle southeast of this kingdom, some hundred and ten li from here. The pool is called Emerald Waves, and the mountain is named Tumbled Rocks. He had a charming daughter of bewitching beauty. He took a Nine-Headed Prince Consort into his household, whose divine powers were unmatched. Knowing of the marvel atop your pagoda, the prince consort conspired with the Dragon King to steal it: first they brought down a rain of blood, and then they made off with the śarīra. Even now it illuminates the dragon palace, making the blackest night as bright as day. The princess secretly employed her powers to steal the Queen Mother’s numinous fungus as well, and uses it in the pool to nurture the treasure. We two are not the ringleaders, but mere soldiers dispatched by the Dragon King. We were captured tonight, and everything we have confessed is true.” The king said, “You have made your confession, but why have you not given your own names?” One monster replied, “I am called Benbo’erba, and he is called Babo’erben. Benbo’erba is a catfish spirit, while Babo’erben is a snakehead spirit.” The king ordered the Embroidered-Uniform Guard to secure them carefully in prison. He then proclaimed, “Remove the cangues and shackles from all the monks of Golden Ray Monastery. Have the Court of Imperial Entertainments quickly prepare a banquet in the Qilin Hall, that we may thank the holy monks for capturing the thieves and discuss asking them to seize the ringleaders.”

p.src: The Court of Imperial Entertainments at once prepared two banquets, one with meat and one vegetarian. The king invited the Tang Monk and his three disciples to take their seats in the Qilin Hall, then asked, “What is your reverend name, holy monk?” The Tang Monk joined his palms and replied, “My family name before ordination was Chen, and my Dharma name is Xuanzang. By imperial grace I was granted the surname Tang, and my humble title is Tripitaka.” The king asked again, “And what are the reverend names of your worthy disciples?” Tripitaka replied, “My humble disciples have no formal titles. The first is named Sun Wukong, the second Zhu Wuneng, and the third Sha Wujing. These names were bestowed by the Bodhisattva Guanyin of the Southern Sea. After they took me as their master, I also called Wukong ‘Pilgrim,’ Wuneng ‘Eight Precepts,’ and Wujing ‘Monk.’” When the king had heard this, he seated Tripitaka in the place of honor, Sun the Pilgrim at the side seat to his left, and Zhu Eight Precepts and Sha the Monk at the side seat to his right. Their fare consisted entirely of vegetarian fruit, vegetables, tea, and rice. At a meat-laden table in front sat the king; below him, at more than a hundred meat-laden tables, sat the many civil and military officials. The ministers thanked their sovereign for his favor, while the disciples asked their master’s pardon, and all took their seats. The king offered wine. Tripitaka dared not drink, but each of his three disciples accepted the welcoming cup. From below came the blended sound of pipes and strings as the Imperial Music Office began to play. Now look at Eight Precepts opening his maw to eat! Like a tiger gulping and a wolf devouring, he polished off every fruit and vegetable on the table. Before long, more soup and rice were brought to replace them, and he ate those without leaving so much as a morsel. Whenever the wine servers came around, he refused not a single cup. The feast continued merrily until it finally dispersed in the afternoon.

p.src: Tripitaka offered thanks for the splendid banquet. The king detained him, saying, “This banquet was merely a small token of gratitude for the holy monks’ feat in capturing the monsters.” He ordered the Court of Imperial Entertainments, “Quickly reset the banquet in Jianzhang Palace. We shall invite the holy monks again to devise a plan for capturing the ringleaders and restoring the treasure to the pagoda.” Tripitaka said, “If the thieves are to be caught and the treasure recovered, there is no need to trouble yourselves with another banquet. We shall take our leave of Your Majesty now and go capture the monsters.” The king would not consent and insisted on inviting them to Jianzhang Palace, where they ate another banquet. Raising his cup, the king asked, “Which holy monk will lead the company forth to subdue and capture the fiends?” Tripitaka replied, “My senior disciple Sun Wukong shall go.” The Great Sage cupped his hands and accepted the charge. The king said, “Since Elder Sun is going, how many troops and horses will he require? When will he leave the city?” Unable to contain himself, Eight Precepts cried aloud, “What need have we of troops and horses? And why should we care what hour it is? Now that we are flushed with wine and full of food, my elder brother and I will go and seize them as soon as we lay hands on them.” Tripitaka was delighted and said, “Eight Precepts has been remarkably diligent of late!” The Pilgrim said, “In that case, let Junior Brother Sha remain to protect Master, while the two of us go and return.” The king asked, “Since you two elders need no troops, will you require weapons?” Eight Precepts laughed. “We cannot use the weapons of your household. We brothers carry our own arms.” Hearing this, the king immediately fetched a great goblet to drink a parting toast to the two elders. The Great Sage Sun said, “We shall drink no more. Just have the Embroidered-Uniform Guard bring out those two lesser fiends, so that we may take them along as guides.” The king issued the order, and they were brought out at once. The two disciples each dragged along one lesser fiend, mounted the wind, employed their transporting magic, and sped straight southeastward. Ah! Of their journey, it may be said:
